stops.title: The Wrigley Building
stops.text: The gleaming white terra-cotta clock tower at the river's edge, finished in 1924. Floodlit every night since it opened, it was modelled on the Giralda tower of Seville's cathedral.

stops.title: Tribune Tower
stops.text: The 1925 winner of the most famous design competition in skyscraper history: a Gothic crown of flying buttresses. Look down at the base, where more than 120 stones from world landmarks are set into the walls.

stops.title: Trump International Hotel & Tower
stops.text: A steel-and-glass tower whose setbacks line up with its neighbours — the Wrigley Building's cornice, Marina City's roofline and 330 North Wabash.

stops.title: Marina City
stops.text: Bertrand Goldberg's 1964 corn cobs: sixteen petal balconies a floor, and nineteen floors of parking spiralling up beneath the apartments. A city within a city, with a marina at the river's edge.

stops.title: The Merchandise Mart
stops.text: When it opened in 1930 it was the largest building in the world by floor area. After dark, Art on the Mart projects moving artwork across its river façade.

stops.title: 110 North Wacker
stops.text: The newest tower on the bend of the river, its fins and curving base following the water where the main stem meets the South Branch.

stops.title: Willis Tower
stops.text: Nine bundled tubes of black aluminium and bronze glass, the tallest building in the Western Hemisphere from 1973 to 1998. The Skydeck's glass Ledge hangs 1,353 feet over Wacker Drive.

stops.title: Buckingham Fountain
stops.text: Chicago's front door on the lake since 1927: pink Georgia marble, four pairs of bronze sea horses for the four lake states, and a centre jet that climbs 150 feet in the water shows.

stops.title: The Field Museum
stops.text: The natural-history museum at the head of Museum Campus, home to SUE, the most complete Tyrannosaurus rex ever found.

stops.title: Shedd Aquarium
stops.text: A 1930 Beaux-Arts temple for 32,000 animals, from beluga whales to sea otters. Its Oceanarium looks straight out over Lake Michigan.

stops.title: Adler Planetarium
stops.text: The first planetarium in the Western Hemisphere, opened in 1930 at the tip of the peninsula. Its lawn gives the widest unobstructed view of the skyline in the city.

stops.title: Soldier Field
stops.text: The Bears' home since 1971, its 1924 Doric colonnades wrapped around a modern bowl — a war memorial first, a stadium second.

stops.title: Northerly Island
stops.text: A former airstrip turned lakefront prairie, with walking paths, a lagoon and the summer concert pavilion under its white tent.

stops.title: 12th Street Beach
stops.text: A small, quiet beach tucked behind the planetarium, facing open water — one of the calmest swims on the lakefront.

stops.title: Art on the Mart
stops.text: After dark the Mart's river façade becomes one of the largest permanent digital art projections in the world, 2.5 acres of moving light.

stops.title: Marina City at night
stops.text: The corn cobs lit from within, their petal balconies stacked like the scales of a pine cone above the river.

stops.title: The Wrigley Building
stops.text: Floodlit white every night since 1921 — the brightest wall on the river.

stops.title: 875 North Michigan
stops.text: The tapering black tower with its X-bracing and twin antennas; its crown lights change colour with the seasons and the city's teams.

stops.title: The Centennial Wheel
stops.text: Navy Pier's 200-foot wheel, lit in shifting colours over the lake and the pier's summer fireworks.

stops.title: The Chicago Theatre
stops.text: The six-storey C-H-I-C-A-G-O sign and its marquee of chasing bulbs, lighting State Street since 1921.

stops.title: Standing Lincoln
stops.text: Saint-Gaudens's twelve-foot Lincoln of 1887, just risen from his chair, before Stanford White's curved granite exedra. The Couch Tomb, last of the old City Cemetery that became this park, stands a short walk north.

stops.title: North Avenue Beach House
stops.text: Built in 1999 as an ocean liner run aground on the sand: a white hull with portholes, a blue-railed deck and two funnels. The Chess Pavilion's carved limestone king and queen stand just to the south.

stops.title: Café Brauer and South Pond
stops.text: Dwight Perkins's 1908 Prairie School refectory curves around South Pond under green tile roofs. Across the water, Studio Gang's honeycomb pavilion rises over the Nature Boardwalk.

stops.title: The Kovler Lion House
stops.text: The heart of one of the oldest free zoos in America: the 1912 Lion House, tapestry brick under a tile roof, its great arched door guarded by terra-cotta lions. The sea lions swim just to the west.

stops.title: Lincoln Park Conservatory
stops.text: Four Victorian glass houses of 1890–95, the Palm House rising fifty feet over the formal garden. At the garden's far end, Saint-Gaudens's Bates Fountain: storks at play among bronze reeds.

stops.title: Alfred Caldwell Lily Pool
stops.text: Caldwell's 1938 prairie river: a slow pool between stratified limestone ledges, a waterfall at its head and a council ring under the trees. A National Historic Landmark hidden in plain sight.

stops.title: Theater on the Lake
stops.text: A 1920 fresh-air sanitarium with sweeping brick arches, a summer theatre since 1953, on the lake at Fullerton. North Pond and the Nature Museum's butterfly haven are a short walk west.

stops.title: Waveland Clock Tower
stops.text: Edwin Clark's 1931 English Gothic carillon tower at the park's northern edge, a clock on every face — and the clubhouse of the Marovitz golf course along the lake.
